prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Time, How, That

outputs.L1:
Time, only cause of my unrest,  
By whom I hoped once to be blessed,  
How cruel art thou turned?  
That first gav’st life unto my love,  
And still a pleasure not to move  
Or change, though ever burned.

Have I thee slackened, or left undone  
One loving rite, and so have won  
Thy rage or bitter changing?  
That now no minutes I shall see  
Wherein I may least happy be,  
Thy favors so estranging.

Blame thyself, and not my folly;  
Time gave time but to be holy.  
True love such ends best loveth;  
Unworthy love doth seek for ends,  
A worthy love but worth pretends,  
Nor other thoughts it proveth.

Then stay thy swiftness, cruel Time,  
And let me once more blessed climb  
To joy, that I may praise thee.  
Let me pleasure sweetly tasting,  
Joy in love, and faith not wasting,  
And on Fame’s wings I’ll raise thee.

Never shall thy glory dying  
Be, until thine own untying,  
That Time no longer liveth.  
’Tis a gain such time to lend,  
Since so thy fame shall never end,  
But joy for what she giveth.
outputs.L2:
Time alone is the source of my disquiet—  
time, from which I once expected happiness.  
How harsh you have become:  
you first gave life to my affection,  
then refused to ease it, alter it,  
or let it rest, though it kept burning.

Have I neglected you?  
Have I failed to perform  
even one devoted act of love,  
and so earned your anger  
or your cruel change of heart?  
Now I can find no single moment  
in which I may be even slightly glad,  
because your kindness has grown so distant.

Do not accuse my foolishness;  
accuse yourself instead.  
Time granted time only so that love  
might remain pure and sacred.  
False love looks for conclusions and rewards;  
true love seeks only what is worthy,  
and proves no other intention.

So restrain your speed, merciless time,  
and allow me once again  
to rise into blessed joy,  
so that I may praise you.  
Let me taste delight sweetly,  
rejoice in love,  
and keep faith unspent;  
then I will lift your name  
on the wings of fame.

Your honor shall never perish  
until your own ending comes—  
until time itself no longer exists.  
It is a gain for you to lend such hours,  
because your renown will then endure forever,  
and joy will bless you  
for what you have given.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents Time as the only cause of his suffering, unrest, and sorrow. Rather than blaming his beloved, himself, or the nature of love, he directs all responsibility toward Time. In his view, Time has created the painful conditions under which he lives: it has allowed his love to exist, but it has not allowed that love to bring him peace or happiness.

Time is therefore portrayed as cruel and unjust. The speaker suggests that Time gave life and growth to his love, only to deny him the fulfillment that should naturally follow. This makes Time seem almost malicious, as though it has encouraged his deepest feelings while withholding the joy that ought to accompany them. His distress comes from this contradiction: love has been awakened in him, but happiness remains out of reach.

The speaker also insists that he has done nothing to deserve such harsh treatment. He claims that he has not failed in any duty of love and has neglected no act of devotion. His love has been sincere, faithful, and complete. Because of this, he believes Time has no reason to punish him. His complaint is not merely that he suffers, but that he suffers unfairly despite having loved worthily.

The poem also presents a broader argument about the nature of true love. Genuine and honorable love, according to the speaker, does not pursue selfish pleasure or base desires. Instead, it seeks holiness, devotion, and moral purity. Worthy love is spiritual as much as emotional; it aims at reverence and faithfulness rather than possession or self-interest. By emphasizing this, the speaker defends the nobility of his own feelings.

In the end, the speaker appeals directly to Time, asking it to slow its course and grant him the joy he longs for in love. He pleads for relief from his sorrow and hopes that Time will allow his devotion to be rewarded. In return, he promises to honor Time with lasting praise. If Time grants him happiness, he will make Time famous forever through his words, preserving its name in poetry and giving it everlasting glory.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents Time as a powerful and almost tyrannical force responsible for the speaker’s suffering and emotional unrest. By addressing Time directly, the speaker uses apostrophe to turn an abstract concept into a figure that can be blamed, challenged, and pleaded with. Time is shown as cruel because it separates the speaker from happiness, love, or peace, and its constant movement prevents the speaker from fully enjoying life’s most precious moments. The speaker therefore begs Time to pause or soften its harshness, hoping for a brief return of joy and affection.

At the same time, the poem suggests that love has the power to transform even Time itself. If Time allows the speaker to experience happiness again, it will not simply be an enemy or destroyer; instead, it will become associated with pleasure, fulfillment, and emotional renewal. The poem ends with the idea that Time can gain lasting fame if it permits love to flourish. In this way, the speaker argues that love gives meaning to human life and even grants value to Time, making it memorable rather than merely destructive. The poem therefore combines complaint, pleading, and praise to show that while Time may cause suffering, love can redeem it and give it enduring significance.
outputs.L5:
**Time, How, and That**

Time is one of the most important parts of life. It moves forward every moment, whether we notice it or not. We use time to plan our days, remember the past, and imagine the future. Sometimes time feels fast, especially when we are happy or busy. At other moments, it feels slow, especially when we are waiting for something important.

How we use our time can shape who we become. If we spend time learning, helping others, and working toward our goals, we can grow in meaningful ways. If we waste time without thinking, we may later wish we had made different choices. This is why it is important to ask ourselves how we want to spend each day.

That is the lesson time teaches us: every moment has value. We cannot go back and change yesterday, but we can decide what to do today. Time reminds us that life is always moving, and how we use it matters.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an original poem in the style of a 17th-century English love lyric, using archaic spelling, addressing Time as a cruel force keeping the speaker from their beloved.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Time, My Tyrant**

O Time, thou churlish thiefe of fairest houres,  
That cropp’st the rose ere Love hath drunke her dew,  
Why dost thou hedge my path with thornie powres,  
And set long dayes betwixt my Love and mew?  

Thou draw’st thy leaden feete through all my smart,  
Yet wing’d thou fly’st when I her presence taste;  
A moment by her side o’er-runs my heart,  
But absent yeares are in one minute plac’d.  

Unkinde old Sire, with glasse and sythe in hand,  
What glory hast thou in a lover’s teares?  
Thou mak’st my sighes thy measure, and thy sand  
Falls thick as sorrow through the emptie yeares.  

O stay thy course, or else more swiftly move;  
Be slow to part, be hastie to restore:  
For whilst thou barr’st me from my onely Love,  
Thou kill’st me dayly, yet I dye no more.  

But if thy frost must whiten all my brow,  
And make my youth a tale that none shall prove,  
Yet this I sweare: thou shalt not conquer now—  
My soule keepes time by her, and not by thee, O Love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Renaissance-style poem where the narrator pleads with Time to slow down so they can enjoy love once more; make it sound like early modern English with irregular spelling.
counterfactuals.output:
O Time, thou gray-beard wth thy glassie wing,  
Stay yet thy steppes, and turne not all to dust;  
Let not thy yron wheele so swiftly spring,  
Nor make my Maye a servant unto rust.  

A little while, good Time, for pittie bide;  
Let Love’s sweete fire re-enkindle in mine eyne.  
The rose that blush’d by my fayre mistris’ side  
Yet breathes, if thou wilt spare one houre of thine.  

Why dost thou plucke the garland from my brow?  
Why chasest mirth, as houndes the trembling deere?  
Soft, soft, olde thief! defer thy furrow’d plow,  
And leave one kissing-season to us heere.  

For when her hand in mine did lately lye,  
The worlde was all an orchard fresh with dew;  
Her voyce could bid the winter cloudes goe by,  
And make dead hopes put forth their leaves anew.  

Then slack thy sandes, or make thy minutes lame;  
Unwind thy clocke, let noone forget to flye.  
I aske not crownes, nor conquest, wealth, nor fame—  
But one more eve beneath my ladie’s eye.  

O Time, if ever thou wert young and kinde,  
If ever Beautie held thy hart in thrall,  
Remember how Love’s fetters pleas’d thy minde,  
And let not night too soon upon us fall.  

So shall I blesse thy name, though hoarie growne,  
And call thee gentle, not our mortall foe;  
If thou wilt leave, ere all my joyes be flowne,  
One lingering houre wherein to love her so.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a metaphysical love poem about unrest, true love, and the cruelty of time, imitating old manuscript orthography and punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Leafe from the Booke of Vnquiet Loue**

Whan Night, with inke-blacke fingers, clos’d the skie,  
And all the windes made mutinie in the deepe,  
My Soule sate waking, though mine eyes would sleepe,  
And ask’d the Starres wherefore true Loue must die.

For Time, that gray and canker-toothed Theefe,  
Stealeth the rose ere yet the bud be red;  
He layeth frost vpon the marriage-bed,  
And writeth dust vpon the greene young leafe.

Yet thou, my Deare, art fixt beyond his spight,  
A lampe within the caues of my despaire;  
Though houres like rauens beat the troubled aire,  
Thy name keepes Sabbath in my heart all night.

O strange vnrest! that maketh peace more pure;  
O blessed wound! that bleedeth and doth blesse;  
In losing thee, I touch Loues endlesnesse,  
And by Time’s crueltie am made secure.

For what he breakes, the Spirit may restore;  
What he doth bury, Heauen may awake;  
And though our mortall formes must bend and shake,  
True Loue hath rootes where clocks can strike no more.

Then let the ages grind their iron wheele,  
Let dust deuoure the beauty of the brow;  
I lou’d thee once, I loue thee euer now—  
A flame no winter of the world can steale.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Jacobean-era sounding poem beginning with “Time only cause of my unrest” and continuing as a lover’s complaint to Time.
counterfactuals.output:
Time only cause of my unrest,  
Thou thief that robb’st me of my dear,  
Why dost thou lodge within my breast  
And beat thy iron minutes here?  

Thou creep’st when I would have thee fly,  
And fliest when she is in mine eye;  
Thy glass runs swift to part our bliss,  
Yet leaden-slow to bring her kiss.  

O crooked lord of youth and age,  
That writ’st our joys in sand and air,  
Blot out one line of thy dark page,  
Or make my lady’s absence fair.  

If thou must steal, steal from my pain;  
If thou must wound, wound not delight;  
Restore the hour she comes again,  
And take a year of this long night.  

But if no prayer thy scythe may stay,  
Nor sighs can bribe thy churlish wing,  
Then haste thee to that happy day  
Wherein her hand my peace shall bring.  

Till then, false Time, my foe remain,  
My jailor, torturer, and guest;  
For every tick renews my chain—  
Time only cause of my unrest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fake early modern English poem in which the speaker accuses Time of estranging love’s favors, then promises to immortalize Time’s glory through praise.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Time**

O Time, thou thief with softly-pacing feet,  
That steal’st the roses from my lady’s cheek,  
And mak’st love’s summer alter, fade, and fleet,  
Till former favours seem estranged and weak;  

Why hast thou set thy frost betwixt our fires,  
And taught sweet eyes to look as though unknown?  
Why dost thou make old vows and young desires  
Stand far apart, as seeds by tempest sown?  

Yet, tyrant, hear: though thou my joy dost waste,  
And turn’st affection’s honey into gall,  
My verse shall bind thee, ere thy self be past,  
And make thy ruin glorious over all.  

For I will praise thy chariot, wheel, and wing,  
Thy glass, thy scythe, thy crown of dust and flame;  
So shalt thou live in what my numbers sing,  
And borrow deathless honour of my name.  

Then rage, if rage thou must; consume, devour:  
Estrange love’s grace, and make bright beauty old.  
I’ll crown thee lord of every vanquish’d hour,  
And in my praise thy endless triumph hold.
